reason: Value P is correct; the citation fails on both venue and object, and I confirmed this from the GHR full text. (1) Venue: Miyano's lfm-subgraph paper is Mathematical Systems Theory 22(1) (1989) 47-73 (conf. version FCT 1987), not IJFCS 1990. (2) Object drift: Miyano's theorem is about the lfm VERTEX set whose INDUCED subgraph satisfies a nontrivial hereditary property — GHR catalogue that result separately as Problem A.2.16 LFMS(pi). Lex-first maximal MATCHING is an edge-set problem and GHR list it in the OPEN PROBLEMS appendix as Problem B.8.2, remarking 'LFMM is NC equivalent to Comparator Circuit Value, Problem B.8.1' and 'A P-completeness proof for LFMM would imply that Edge-weighted Matching, Problem B.1.3, is also P-complete'; GHR's A.2.21 remark adds 'for k = 1 this problem becomes Lexicographically First Maximal Matching, Problem B.8.2; it is in CC'. So Miyano's theorem provably does not cover this cell. GHR's own reference for B.8.2 is Mayr and Subramanian, whose abstract (verified from the Stanford tech report STAN-CS-89-1278) states CC 'contains several natural complete problems, including Circuit Value for comparator circuits, Lex-first Maximal Matching'; with NL ⊆ CC ⊆ P this places LFMM in P.
corrected_citation: E. W. Mayr & A. Subramanian, The complexity of circuit value and network stability, Journal of Computer and System Sciences 44(2) (1992) 302-323 (lex-first maximal matching is CC-complete, and NL ⊆ CC ⊆ P, hence LFMM is in P); see also S. Cook, Y. Filmus & D. T. M. Le, The complexity of the comparator circuit value problem, ACM Transactions on Computation Theory 7(4) (2015), Article 19

reason: Value P is correct, and GHR's own text settles the citation question. GHR Problem A.6.1 'Unit Resolution (UNIT)' reads: 'Reference: Jones and Laaser [181]. Hint: Jones and Laaser provide a polynomial time algorithm for unit resolution [181].' GHR are explicitly relaying, not establishing — the poly-time unit-propagation algorithm and the log-space P-completeness are both Jones & Laaser's. GHR bibliography entry [181] is the 1976 TCS paper.
corrected_citation: N. D. Jones & W. T. Laaser, Complete problems for deterministic polynomial time, Theoretical Computer Science 3(1) (1976) 105-117 (polynomial-time algorithm for unit resolution; UNIT is log-space complete for P)

reason: The canonical_task conjoins order-independence with poly-time, and the citation supports only the first half. Bjorner-Lovasz-Shor (1991) establish the abelian property (finiteness and the terminating configuration are independent of the order of moves) and the chip-count thresholds (N < |E| always finite; N > 2|E|-|V| always infinite). The polynomial bound the value P depends on is Tardos's, and her abstract says so in as many words: 'Bjorner, Lovasz, and Shor have introduced a chip firing game on graphs. This paper proves a polynomial bound on the length of the game in terms of the number of vertices of the graph provided the length is finite. The obtained bound is best possible within a constant factor.' Tardos (1988) predates the BLS journal paper and is universally cited as the separate source of the O(n^4) firing bound, so a two-part citation is required.
corrected_citation: G. Tardos, Polynomial bound for a chip firing game on graphs, SIAM Journal on Discrete Mathematics 1(3) (1988) 397-398 (polynomial, O(n^4), bound on the length of a terminating game, tight up to a constant factor), together with A. Bjorner, L. Lovasz & P. W. Shor, Chip-firing games on graphs, European Journal of Combinatorics 12(4) (1991) 283-291 (order-independence / abelian property)

reason: Wrong paper, confirmed against the GHR compendium. GHR Problem A.12.6 is exactly this object — 'Lempel-Ziv Data Compression (LZDC): Is string t added to the dictionary when string s is encoded using the LZ2 coding algorithm?' — and its 'Reference:' line is De Agostino [79] = 'P-complete problems in data compression, Theoretical Computer Science 127:181-186, 1994', with the remark that De Agostino also proves the next-character and first-character heuristics P-complete. The cited De Agostino & Storer IPL 59 (1996) 169-174 paper is a different result (NP-completeness of computing the OPTIMAL parsing, plus a lower bound on on-line approximability) — a hardness result about a neighbouring object, not the greedy LZ78 parse being poly-time. GHR's bibliography entry [80] for De Agostino & Storer is their 1992 DCC parallel-dictionary paper, not the IPL one either.
corrected_citation: J. Ziv & A. Lempel, Compression of individual sequences via variable-rate coding, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 24(5) (1978) 530-536 (the incremental/greedy LZ78 dictionary parse, linear time); for the exact placement inside P see S. De Agostino, P-complete problems in data compression, Theoretical Computer Science 127(1) (1994) 181-186 (LZ2/LZ78 greedy compression and two standard variations are P-complete, hence in P)

reason: Verified against the GHR full text. Problem A.2.6 'Lexicographically First Delta+1 Vertex Coloring (LFDVC)' states exactly the canonical_task (given G, a vertex ordering, a colour c and a vertex v, is v coloured c in the lexicographically least Delta+1 colouring?) and is catalogued as P-complete. Crucially GHR are not merely relaying: the entry's Reference is '(Michael Luby, Personal Communication, 1984), Luby [246]', i.e. the primary is an unpublished personal communication, and GHR themselves supply the proof — the Hint gives the full reduction from NANDCVP (Problem A.1.5), gate-by-gate construction included, plus the observation that the lexicographically least colouring is computable in polynomial time by greedy scan. GHR is therefore the citable establishing source, and there is no better published primary to substitute.

Garey & Johnson (1979) list SUBGRAPH ISOMORPHISM as [GT48] and state NP-completeness for exactly the decision form given (is H isomorphic to a subgraph of G?). Problem-ID-level match with the canonical_task; the note correctly separates induced-subgraph-isomorphism and graph-isomorphism.

Garey & Johnson, SIAM J. Comput. 4 (1975) 397-411, is the primary source in which 3-PARTITION is proved strongly NP-complete (NP-complete with all integers bounded by a polynomial in m, i.e. under unary encoding) — exactly the stated canonical_task and exactly the property the note relies on. The [SP15] pointer is a correct secondary cross-reference, and the note correctly distinguishes weakly-NP-complete Partition.

Papadimitriou, Computing 16 (1976) 263-270, is the primary NP-completeness proof and its title is the theorem: the NP-completeness of the bandwidth minimization problem, i.e. is there a layout of bandwidth <= b. Same object, same value; cutwidth/MinLA correctly split off in the note.

Fellows, Rosamond, Rotics & Szeider, SIAM J. Discrete Math. 23(2) (2009) 909-939 (STOC 2006), is the primary source and the title is the theorem: 'Clique-width is NP-complete', for precisely the decision cwd(G) <= k. No drift; treewidth and rank-width correctly split off.

Garey & Johnson, SIAM J. Algebraic Discrete Methods 4(3) (1983) 312-316, titled 'Crossing number is NP-complete', is the primary proof for exactly the stated decision problem (a drawing with <= k crossings?). Rectilinear crossing number correctly split off in the note.

Value NPC is right; neither cited work establishes it for the stated object. Cornuejols-Nemhauser-Wolsey (1990) is a survey chapter (Discrete Location Theory, pp. 119-171) covering general UFL — Guha & Khuller's own abstract cites it exactly that way ('Applications to bank account location and clustering, as well as many related pieces of work, are discussed by Cornuejols, Nemhauser and Wolsey') — and Garey & Johnson (1979) has no metric UFL entry. The canonical_task pins the METRIC case, and Guha & Khuller prove hardness there in their own paper: their abstract states 'We also show that the problem is Max SNP-hard', which gives NP-hardness of metric UFL under P != NP. (Their 1.463 factor lower bound is separate and rests on the stronger NP not-subset-of DTIME[n^{O(log log n)}] assumption, as Jain-Mahdian-Markakis-Saberi-Vazirani and Shmoys's survey both record — so cite the Max SNP-hardness, not the 1.463 bound, for the NP-completeness cell.)
corrected_citation: S. Guha & S. Khuller, Greedy strikes back: Improved facility location algorithms, Journal of Algorithms 31(1) (1999) 228-248 (prelim. version SODA 1998, 649-657) — the metric uncapacitated facility location problem is Max SNP-hard, hence NP-hard

reason: Verified against the paper's full text. Clark, Colbourn & Johnson, Discrete Math. 86 (1990) 165-177, abstract: 'We show that many standard graph theoretic problems remain NP-complete on unit disk graphs, including coloring, independent set, domination, independent domination, and connected domination.' Their Table 1 marks INDEPENDENT SET for unit disk graphs with [*] (proved in this paper), and the text gives Theorem 4.1 (UD VERTEX COVER is NP-complete, by reduction from planar vertex cover of max degree 3) together with the observation that min vertex cover and max independent set are polynomially equivalent on any graph class. Exactly the stated graph class and decision problem.

Garey & Johnson (1979) is the correct establishing source and I confirmed the attribution against two independent peer-reviewed papers that state the exact decision problem. Pandey-Panda-style survey work (arXiv:2002.00002) writes: 'InDM. Question: Does there exist an InDS of size at most l in G? Garey and Johnson [7] have proved that InDM as NP-complete', with [7] = Computers and Intractability (1979); the MinIDS local-search literature (arXiv:1802.06478) likewise cites 'The problem is NP-hard [6]' with [6] = Garey & Johnson 1979. Object matches: unrestricted graphs, independent dominating set, cardinality bound.

Verified against the paper's full text. Formann & Wagner, SoCG 1991, 281-288, Section 5 'NP-completeness result', Theorem 7: 'Problem R4 is NP-complete even if all rectangles are squares of the same size' — R4 being exactly the common-label-size decision. Lemma 8 adds the factor-2 approximation lower bound under P != NP. Same object as canonical_task. (Note for any approximation cell on this problem: Lemma 8 is a constant-factor / APX-hardness bound, not inapprox.)

Boria, Della Croce & Paschos, Discrete Applied Mathematics 196 (2015) 62-71, is devoted to exactly MAX MIN VERTEX COVER (a minimal vertex cover of maximum size). Their abstract claims an in-paper hardness result — a polynomial n^{-1/2}-approximation together with 'unless P = NP, the problem is inapproximable within ratio n^{eps-1/2} for any strictly positive eps' — and a P != NP inapproximability result for the optimisation problem establishes NP-hardness of the stated decision version within the same paper, so this is not a repeated claim. (Flag for any approximation cell on this problem: the n^{eps-1/2} form is a poly-APX-shaped bound, not inapprox.)

Verified against the paper's own abstract: 'we show that 2-MCSP (and therefore MCSP) is NP-hard and, moreover, even APX-hard'. Goldstein, Kolman & Zheng, Electron. J. Combin. 12 (2005) R50 (prelim. ISAAC 2004), is the primary hardness source and treats exactly the canonical_task object (a common partition into <= k blocks), including the each-letter-twice restriction the note records.

Verified against the paper's full text. Blum, Chalasani, Coppersmith, Pulleyblank, Raghavan & Sudan, STOC 1994, 163-171, prove hardness in-paper, not by citation: 'this connection shows that the MLT problem is NP-hard even in the case where the metric space is a plane. For general metric spaces, it is possible to reduce the TSP where all distances are either 1 or 2 (a metric space) to the MLT, in conjunction with the MAX SNP-hardness of the TSP(1,2) problem'. That establishes NP-hardness of the stated decision problem on metric spaces.

Berlekamp, McEliece & van Tilborg, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 24(3) (1978) 384-386, prove that maximum-likelihood decoding of a linear code — their COSET WEIGHTS problem, is there a codeword within Hamming distance d of y — is NP-complete. This is precisely the canonical_task, and the paper is the universally cited primary.

Lewis & Yannakakis, JCSS 20(2) (1980) 219-230, prove node-deletion is NP-complete for EVERY nontrivial property hereditary on induced subgraphs — the title is the theorem. Planarity is hereditary on induced subgraphs and nontrivial (infinitely many graphs have it, infinitely many do not), so the theorem applies with no interpretive step beyond checking those two conditions. Same object: unrestricted graphs, vertex deletion, cardinality bound k.

Verified against the publisher's own abstract for Griggs & Yeh, SIAM J. Discrete Math. 5(4) (1992) 586-595, whose closing sentence is: 'Determining lambda(G) is shown to be NP-complete by relating it to the problem of finding Hamilton paths.' Exactly the stated L(2,1) span decision on unrestricted graphs, proved in-paper.

Garey & Johnson (1979) [SP4] SET SPLITTING is the standard compendium entry for exactly this feasibility problem (equivalently hypergraph 2-colourability / Property B), stated NP-complete and remaining so for sets of size 3. Problem-ID-level match with the canonical_task; the Lovasz attribution in the note is correct.

Berger & Leighton, J. Comput. Biol. 5(1) (1998) 27-40 — the title is the theorem — prove NP-completeness of exactly the HP-model folding decision problem: a self-avoiding embedding of an H/P string achieving at least k H-H contacts, in the cubic lattice. Same object and same scoring function as canonical_task, which does not restrict the lattice.

Garey & Johnson [GT11] PARTITION INTO TRIANGLES is NP-complete, and the step to the packing form is the identity instance with k = n/3 (G partitions into triangles iff G has n/3 vertex-disjoint triangles). That is a tight one-line equivalence, not interpretive charity, and the note already flags the exact-vs-packing relation explicitly.

Bruno, Coffman & Sethi, Comm. ACM 17(7) (1974) 382-387, is the primary and universally used source for the NP-hardness of P2||sum w_j C_j (weighted mean flow time on two identical parallel machines, by reduction from Partition). It establishes the value for P||sum w_j C_j since m=2 is a special case, and the note correctly separates the poly-time single-machine WSPT case.

Edmonds, Canad. J. Math. 17 (1965) 449-467, is the blossom algorithm paper: it gives the polynomial-time algorithm for maximum matching in general graphs, which is exactly the poly-time half of the canonical_task (existence being trivial). Correct object for the decoupling witness (optimisation easy, counting hard).
